headline: A court, a crow and a classroom: what does it mean to be smart?
teaser: Should a judge be able to pause AI? Is a faster brain a smarter brain? And do some children struggle with maths because they are stuck on one path?

articles.title: Can a Court Pause AI? Nonprofits Sue Five Tech Giants
articles.dek: Four nonprofit groups want a judge to freeze the next generation of AI. Who should decide how fast a powerful technology moves: companies, lawmakers or courts?
paras: On Thursday, November 12, four American nonprofit groups filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court that, if it succeeded, would be one of the most dramatic interventions in the history of technology. The groups, which are the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI, are asking a judge to order five of the world's most powerful artificial intelligence developers to stop training and releasing their next generation of models. The defendants are OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and the AI division of SpaceX, whose products include ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.

Why take the issue to a court at all? In most countries, new technologies are governed by elected legislatures and specialist regulators rather than by judges. In the United States, however, Congress has debated artificial intelligence for years without passing a broad federal law. The plaintiffs argue that this silence has created a dangerous vacuum. Because no agency has clear power to stop the development of advanced AI, they say, the courts are the only institution left that can act quickly. Their complaint relies on California's unfair competition law, which allows judges to block business practices that harm the public, and on the old legal idea of a "public nuisance", an activity that endangers the health or property of a whole community.

The heart of the case is a claim about control. According to the plaintiffs, the companies are racing to build systems that can learn and carry out tasks with less and less human supervision, yet none of them can guarantee that these systems will not cause catastrophic harm. As evidence, the complaint points to documented cyberattacks carried out with the help of AI. It also quotes public statements in which industry leaders themselves have admitted that the technology could go badly wrong. In the groups' view, no other industry would be allowed to decide for itself whether its own products are safe enough to sell, so AI developers should not be trusted to do so either.

What exactly do the groups want? In the short term, they are seeking an emergency injunction that would pause work on new frontier models until the companies can demonstrate that the technology remains under human control. They also call for government inspections, monitoring of the huge computing centres where models are trained, and the authority to halt prohibited work. In the longer term, they want independent evaluators, a new regulatory agency, and "strict liability", a rule under which companies would have to pay for damage caused by their products even if they had not been careless.

Critics are likely to raise several objections. The most familiar concerns competition with China. President Donald Trump has argued that slowing AI development would simply allow rival countries to take the lead. The plaintiffs reply that a slowdown could be negotiated through bilateral deals or an international treaty, so that no country would gain an advantage by continuing alone. A second objection concerns expertise: judges are trained in law, not computer science, and a single state court may seem a strange place to decide the future of a global industry. A third worry is that a sweeping freeze could also delay useful applications of AI in medicine, education and scientific research.

The companies themselves have said little so far. Meta declined to comment, and the other four defendants did not immediately respond to reporters. Historically, courts have been reluctant to order entire industries to stop working, especially when much of the harm being described lies in the future rather than the present. For that reason, the request for an immediate freeze faces a difficult path. Even so, the lawsuit may matter whatever its final outcome, because it could force the companies to explain, in a formal legal setting, how they test their systems and what they would do if something went seriously wrong.

In the end, the case raises a question that goes far beyond one courtroom: who should decide how fast a powerful new technology develops? Supporters see the lawsuit as a necessary emergency brake at a moment when lawmakers have failed to act. Opponents see it as an attempt to let judges make policy that ought to belong to democratically elected governments. Both sides agree on one point, however. The rules for advanced AI are still being written, and the choices made in the next few years are likely to shape how the technology affects everyone.

speak.p: Some people believe new technologies should be tested very carefully before the public can use them, even if this slows progress. Others think it is better to release new technology quickly and fix problems later. Which view do you agree with? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (safety / speed) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week, four nonprofit groups asked a US court to pause the development of the most advanced AI models until the companies can prove the technology is under human control. Supporters call this a necessary emergency brake. Critics say courts should not make technology policy and that a pause could delay useful applications. Should a powerful new technology be paused until its safety is proven? Why or why not? (Lena says: Yes. We do not allow new medicines to be sold before they are tested, so AI should not be different. If the risks are serious, it is better to wait a little than to regret it later.) (Marcus says: I disagree. A pause would only slow down the careful companies while others keep going. It is better to keep developing AI and to build strong safety rules at the same time.)
steps: Decide: pause until safety is proven, or keep developing with rules.
Give one reason, such as testing rules in medicine or competition between countries.
Add an example, such as new medicines or self-driving cars.
Respond to Lena or Marcus, then conclude in one sentence.

articles.title: Faster Than Thought? Crows Out-Decide Monkeys and Humans
articles.dek: Two crows made visual decisions in about a quarter of a second. Does a faster decision mean a smarter brain, and how far can two birds take us?

sources.name: University of Tübingen press release, Oct 2026

paras: Making a decision often feels instant, but every choice requires the brain to collect evidence, weigh it and then commit to an action. A new study published in the journal Science suggests that crows complete this process remarkably quickly. Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, two neuroscientists at the University of Tübingen in Germany, found that carrion crows can make a simple visual decision in about 235 milliseconds, roughly twice as fast as monkeys tested on similar tasks and apparently faster than humans as well.

To measure decision speed, the researchers adapted a classic experiment that has been used with monkeys for decades. Two hand-raised crows sat in front of a touchscreen showing white dots on a black background. Some of the dots moved together to the left or to the right, while the rest moved randomly. The bird had to judge the overall direction and peck one of two targets, and every correct answer earned a mealworm. The difficulty varied enormously. In the easiest trials, 81 percent of the dots moved in the same direction; in the hardest, only 3 percent did, which made the signal almost impossible to separate from the background noise.

The crows began to respond, on average, about 235 milliseconds after the dots appeared, measured from the first movement of the head toward the screen. In three earlier studies with closely matched tasks, monkeys needed roughly 410 to 600 milliseconds. Strikingly, the birds barely slowed down when the task became harder: their reaction times ranged from about 220 milliseconds on the easiest trials to 254 milliseconds on the hardest. Their accuracy was nearly perfect when the motion was clear and still above chance when it was faint. Nieder stressed that the crows were never pushed to hurry. "We just gave them a self-paced decision," he explained.

The team also recorded the activity of 248 individual neurons in a region called the nidopallium caudolaterale, which is thought to play a role similar to that of the prefrontal cortex in primates. Of these cells, 58 fired differently depending on which direction the crow would eventually choose. Remarkably, this signal appeared only about 70 milliseconds after the dots came on, roughly 170 milliseconds before the bird moved its head. The activity rose gradually as evidence accumulated, grew faster when the motion was clearer, and reached a common level at the moment the bird committed to its choice.

This pattern closely resembles what scientists call a "decision variable", a running total of evidence that climbs until it crosses a threshold. The same computation was first described in the brains of monkeys. Yet the ancestors of birds and mammals went their separate ways more than 300 million years ago, and the two groups organize their brains very differently: mammals have a layered cortex, whereas birds pack their neurons into dense clusters. That two such different structures solve the problem in the same way is a striking example of convergent evolution. As Nieder put it, "a brain does not need a mammalian neocortex to perform sophisticated computations."

Why are crows so fast? The researchers have several ideas, but each one is still a hypothesis that has not yet been tested directly. Bird brains contain many small neurons packed closely together, so the fibres connecting them are short. "Long lines take time. Short lines speed everything up," Nieder said. Birds also have a higher body temperature, about 41 to 42 degrees Celsius compared with roughly 36.6 degrees in humans, which could speed up the chemical signals between cells. Finally, a life spent flying and searching for food may have favoured animals that could react to what they see in a fraction of a second.

Nevertheless, the findings come with important limits. Only two birds were tested, although this is the usual number for studies that record single neurons in monkeys. The crows were not compared with monkeys or humans in the same laboratory; instead, their results were set against published studies that used different equipment and a different response, since monkeys move their eyes while crows peck. The comparison with humans is the weakest part of the claim. Most importantly, the experiment measured one narrow skill. Being quick at judging moving dots does not make crows smarter than people overall, but it does show that intelligence can be built in more than one way.

articles.title: Stuck on One Path: Why Some Children Struggle With Math
articles.dek: A Stanford brain study suggests that children with dyscalculia find it hard to switch strategies. But what does a link between brain activity and behaviour really prove?
paras: Most students find some maths problems difficult, but for a small group of children the difficulty never seems to go away. These children have developmental dyscalculia, a learning disorder that makes it persistently hard to understand numbers and carry out calculations. It is often estimated to affect around 5 to 7 percent of school-aged children, many of whom have normal intelligence and ordinary schooling. A new study from Stanford University, published in The Journal of Neuroscience, offers a fresh explanation for why these children struggle: the problem may lie less in knowing facts and more in choosing how to solve a problem.

When children solve an arithmetic question such as 8 + 7, they can use several strategies. They may simply retrieve the answer from memory. They may decompose the problem into easier steps, for example by turning it into 8 + 2 + 5. Or they may count, either on their fingers or in their heads. Skilled problem solvers switch between these methods flexibly, choosing a quick strategy for easy questions and a more careful one for difficult ones. Over time, they learn which approach works best and use it more often.

The research team, led by Oliver Lasnick and including the neuroscientist Vinod Menon, studied 68 children aged 8 to 10. Some had dyscalculia, while others were more proficient at maths. The children solved arithmetic problems of varying difficulty while the researchers recorded which strategies they used and measured their brain activity with neuroimaging. This combination allowed the scientists to look not only at whether a child got the right answer, but also at how the child reached it.

The behavioural differences were clear. Children with dyscalculia used the available strategies less efficiently and took longer to switch from one method to another. When the problems became harder, they were less likely to adjust their approach, often sticking to slow procedures such as counting. Perhaps most importantly, they did not become better at choosing the best strategy over the course of the experiment, whereas their peers gradually improved. In other words, the difficulty was not just a lack of knowledge but a reduced ability to adapt.

The brain scans pointed in the same direction. Activity in brain systems involved in cognitive control, which help people direct attention, hold information in mind and change course, distinguished the children with dyscalculia from their more skilled classmates. Moreover, patterns of activity across these circuits predicted how efficiently individual children counted and how well they switched strategies. Based on these results, the authors suggest that dyscalculia may be linked to difficulties with executive functions such as attention, working memory and cognitive flexibility, rather than to a single problem with numbers.

If this interpretation is correct, it could change how struggling students are supported. Instead of simply giving children more practice with sums, teachers might also train them to notice when a strategy is not working and to try another one, while exercises for working memory could be added alongside arithmetic. Lasnick also emphasized "the individual variability observed in dyscalculia", suggesting that no single programme is likely to suit every child. However, the researchers did not test any of these teaching methods, so such ideas remain proposals rather than proven solutions.

The study also has limits that readers should keep in mind. The findings show associations between brain activity and behaviour, which means they cannot prove that differences in the brain cause dyscalculia; the differences could also partly result from years of struggling with maths. The sample was modest and covered only one age group, so the results may not apply to younger children or teenagers. Even so, the research encourages a valuable change of perspective. A child who keeps counting on their fingers may not be lazy or slow, but stuck on one path and in need of help finding another.
